Chapter 10
Access Lists

This manual replaces Chapter 10 of CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (Exam 200-301) by Todd Lammle (2020), book pages 289 to 318. It follows the book's order. It adds simple explanations, command breakdowns, labs and quizzes, and it marks every place where this document differs from the book.

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Learning objectives. The book lists one exam topic for this chapter: 5.6 Configure and verify access control lists (under 5.0 Security Fundamentals). It does not list separate learning objectives. The objectives below are derived from the chapter's Exam Essentials. ADDED
After this chapter you should be able to:
1. Explain what an ACL is and the three rules a packet follows (in order, stop at first match, implicit deny).
2. Choose the right ACL type and number range (standard 1-99 and 1300-1999, extended 100-199 and 2000-2699, or named).
3. Write wildcard masks for a host, a subnet and a range of subnets.
4. Write standard, extended and named ACLs and apply them to an interface in the right direction and place.
5. Protect the VTY lines with an ACL and access-class.
6. Verify ACLs with show access-lists and show ip interface.
VERIFY

Verification note. Every wildcard, range and subnet answer in this document was calculated with a Python script (ipaddress module) and compared with the manual block-size method. The first-match behaviour of the ACL examples was also simulated with a small script. No command here was run on real Cisco equipment or in Packet Tracer. Command outputs are illustrative and tagged CHECK .

- Every ACL ends with a hidden rule. What is it and what does it do? Confidence: K / U / G
- A standard ACL looks at which part of a packet? Confidence: K / U / G
- What is the wildcard mask that matches the same addresses as subnet mask 255.255.255.0? Confidence: K / U / G
- Where should you place an extended ACL, near the source or near the destination? Confidence: K / U / G
- Which command shows you which interface an ACL is applied to? Confidence: K / U / G
BOOK Book page 290. Medium and large networks use layers of security. Three kinds of device show up in the drawing (Figure 10.1):
| Device | Job | Where it sits |
| Perimeter router | First device on your side of the Internet link. Filters traffic coming in from the untrusted network. | Between the Internet and the firewall |
| Firewall | Inspects traffic between the Internet, the DMZ and the inside network. | Behind the perimeter router |
| Internal router | Screens traffic going into parts of the trusted network. It uses access lists to do this. | Between the firewall and the inside LAN |

Two terms you must know: the trusted network (your corporate LAN) and the untrusted network (the Internet). The DMZ (demilitarized zone) is a small separate area that holds servers the outside world must reach, such as web, DNS and email. The book says DMZ addresses can be public (global) or private, depending on how the firewall is set up.
BOOK On the inside, you can use VLANs on switches instead of routers. Multilayer switches that have their own security features can sometimes replace internal routers and give better performance.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says in the next section that Cisco sells "the new Firepower and Firepower Threat Defense (FTD)". Cisco has renamed these. Firepower Threat Defense is now Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense, and the Firepower Management Center is now the Secure Firewall Management Center. Cisco's own Secure Firewall pages show the mapping. The ASA line is still called Secure Firewall ASA. Verification: official Cisco pages.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED A router ACL is a stateless packet filter. It looks at each packet alone and does not remember connections. A real firewall is stateful: it remembers that an inside host started a connection and lets the reply back in. With an ACL you must permit the return traffic yourself. Keep this in mind when you write ACLs later in the chapter.
Quick check 10.1
Q1. In the drawing, which device uses access lists to screen traffic into the trusted network?
Answer: The internal router - the book says internal routers add security by screening traffic with ACLs.
Q2. Where would you normally find the web and email servers that the Internet must reach?
A. The trusted LAN
B. The DMZ
C. Inside the perimeter router
D. On the console port
Answer: B - the DMZ holds the Internet-facing servers.
Q3. Does a router ACL remember that an inside host opened a connection?
Answer: No - an ACL is stateless. A stateful firewall remembers connections. ADDED

BOOK Book pages 291 to 294. An access list is a list of conditions that sort packets. Think of it as a set of if-then statements: if the packet matches this condition, then do this action (permit or deny). If it does not match, go to the next line.
An ACL does nothing until you apply it to an interface (or to a VTY line) in a direction, in or out. Creating the list is only half the job.
The three rules every packet follows
EXAM CRITICAL
1. The packet is compared with the lines in order, from line 1 down.
2. The packet is compared only until the first match. After a match the router acts on it and stops.
3. At the end of every ACL there is an implicit deny. A packet that matches nothing is dropped. You cannot see this line.
How an ACL is processed
Packet arrives
-> line 1 matches? yes: do its action (permit or deny) and STOP
-> no: line 2 matches? yes: do its action and STOP
-> no: ... keep going down the list
-> no line matched: implicit deny (packet dropped)
COMMON MISTAKE

Order matters. If permit ip any any is above a more specific deny line, the deny line is never reached. The packet matches the permit first and stops. Section 10.5 shows a real example of this in the book's own output.
Types of ACL
| Type | What it checks | Number ranges |
| Standard | Source IP address only. It permits or denies a whole suite of protocols. It cannot tell web from Telnet. | 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999 |
| Extended | Source and destination IP, the IP protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP and so on) and the TCP or UDP port number. | 100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699 |
| Named | Not a third type. It is a standard or extended ACL that you create and refer to by name instead of number. | Name (or a number used as a name) |
EXAM CRITICAL
Memorise the number ranges. Standard: 1-99, 1300-1999. Extended: 100-199, 2000-2699. The router reads the number to know which syntax to expect.
Inbound and outbound
| Direction | When the router checks the list | What a deny does |
| Inbound (in) | As the packet arrives on the interface, before the routing decision. | The packet is dropped before it is routed. |
| Outbound (out) | After the router has chosen the exit interface, before the packet is queued out. | The packet is dropped just before it leaves. |
Rules and guidelines from the book
| Guideline | Why it matters |

| One ACL per interface, per protocol, per direction. | You can have one inbound and one outbound IP ACL on an interface. A second one replaces the first. Two lists in the same direction would make the second useless, because of the implicit deny. |
| Put more specific tests at the top. | First match wins, so a broad line placed first hides the narrow lines below it. |
| New lines go at the bottom. | You cannot insert a line in the middle of a classic numbered list. See the update below. |
| Every list needs at least one permit. | A list with only deny lines blocks everything, because of the implicit deny. |
| Create the lines first, then apply the list. | An ACL that is applied but has no lines does not filter anything. |
| ACLs filter traffic going through the router, not traffic the router itself starts. | Packets that the router generates are not checked by its own outbound ACL. |
| Standard ACL: place it close to the destination. | A standard ACL only sees the source address. Near the source it would also block that source from everything else. |
| Extended ACL: place it close to the source. | It can be specific, so stop unwanted traffic early before it wastes bandwidth. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says you cannot remove one line from a numbered ACL, and that named ACLs are the only exception. This is only true for the global access-list command. Cisco's own documentation says sequence numbers work with named and numbered, standard and extended ACLs. To edit a numbered ACL, enter its mode with ip access-list extended 110 (or standard 10) and then use sequence numbers, for example no 20. The book's own named-ACL example in 10.4.4 does exactly this with ACL 110. Verification: official Cisco documentation (Refining an IP Access List) plus a secondary source for the global-command behaviour. Test on your device version. CHECK
WARNING
ADDED ACLs are also used for things other than filtering, for example to pick which addresses NAT translates (Chapter 11). Do not be surprised to meet an ACL that is not applied to an interface.
Quick check 10.2
Q1. A packet matches line 2 of a 5-line ACL. Are lines 3 to 5 checked?
Answer: No - the first match decides and the router stops.
Q2. An ACL has only deny lines. What happens to a packet that matches none of them?
Answer: It is dropped - the implicit deny at the end drops it. A list of only deny lines permits nothing.
Q3. Which of these is an extended ACL number? 55, 150, 1400, 2800
Answer: B - 150 is in 100-199. 55 and 1400 are standard. 2800 is outside every range in this chapter.
Q4. You apply two different ACLs inbound on the same interface, one after the other. How many are active?
Answer: One - the second ip access-group command replaces the first.
10.2.1 Mitigating Security Issues with ACLs

BOOK Book pages 294 and 295. The most common attack is denial of service (DoS). ACLs can help a little, but you really need an IDS or IPS, or a next-generation firewall (NGFW), to stop DoS attacks. The book lists threats that ACLs can help reduce:
- IP address spoofing, inbound and outbound
- DoS TCP SYN attacks (blocking external attacks, or using TCP Intercept)
- DoS smurf attacks
- Denying or filtering ICMP messages, inbound and outbound
- Denying or filtering traceroute
The book says it is not an introduction to security, so you may need to research those terms. That is fair: this chapter only names them.
EXAM CRITICAL
Rules for ACLs from the Internet to your network. Deny packets that arrive from outside but claim a source address that should never come from outside:
1. Any source address from your own internal networks.
2. Local host addresses: 127.0.0.0/8.
3. Private (RFC 1918) addresses.
4. The IP multicast range: 224.0.0.0/4.
| Range | Wildcard form (script-checked) |
Example anti-spoofing ACL ADDED CHECK
ip access-list extended FROM-INTERNET
permit ip any any
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
ip access-group FROM-INTERNET in
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED This is a teaching example, not a complete edge policy. You would also deny your own public address blocks as sources, and the final permit ip any any is far too open for a real edge. If your provider uses private addresses on the link itself, check before you apply it. CHECK
Quick check 10.2.1
Q1. Name two kinds of source address that should never arrive from the Internet.
Answer: Any two of: your own internal addresses, 127.0.0.0/8, RFC 1918 private addresses, 224.0.0.0/4 multicast - the book lists all four.
Q2. Does an ACL alone stop a DoS attack?
Answer: No - the book says you really need an IDS/IPS or an NGFW. ACLs only help a little.
Q3. What wildcard mask matches the whole 172.16.0.0/12 private block?
Answer: B - a /12 leaves 20 host bits, so the second octet wildcard is 15 and the last two are 255. Script-checked.

BOOK Book pages 295 to 303. A standard ACL checks only the source IP address. You create it with an access-list number from 1 to 99 or 1300 to 1999. The number tells the router which syntax to expect, so it will only accept a source address in each line.
The book shows the access-list ? help screen. It lists many protocol ranges. Most are old.
| Range | Meaning (from the book) | Today |
| 1-99 | IP standard | Use |
| 100-199 | IP extended | Use |
| 1300-1999 | IP standard (expanded range) | Use |
| 2000-2699 | IP extended (expanded range) | Use |
| 200-299, 700-799, 1100-1199 | Protocol type-code and 48-bit MAC address lists | Rare. Not on the CCNA exam as far as the outline shows. |
| 300-399, 800-999, 1000-1099, 1200-1299 | DECnet and IPX lists | Obsolete. The book itself says IPX and DECnet are no longer used. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED Ignore the IPX and DECnet ranges. The four IP ranges in the first four rows are the ones to learn. The ranges were checked against the book's own help output and Exam Essentials. They were not re-checked on an official Cisco page in this session. CHECK
Building a standard ACL line
Two lines of a standard ACL BOOK
Corp(config)#access-list 10 deny host 172.16.30.2
Corp(config)#access-list 10 permit any
- access-list creates one numbered line in global configuration mode.
- 10 is the ACL number. 1-99 tells the router this is a standard list.
- deny or permit is the action.
- host 172.16.30.2 means exactly one source address. It is the same as 172.16.30.2 0.0.0.0.
- any means every source address. It is the same as 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255.
Illustrative output CHECK
Corp#show access-lists
Standard IP access list 10
20 permit any

You have three ways to name the source: any, host a.b.c.d, or an address plus a wildcard mask for a range. If you type a single address with no host and no mask, the router assumes host. In your running-config it will appear as host.
MEMORY TIP
No ACL line has a destination in a standard list. If you need to say where the traffic is going, you need an extended ACL.
10.3.1 Wildcard Masking
BOOK Book pages 296 to 298. A wildcard mask tells the router which bits of the address to check and which to ignore. It is used with the address in an ACL line.
EXAM CRITICAL
In a wildcard mask: 0 means the bit must match. 1 means the bit does not matter. This is the opposite of a subnet mask, which is why it is also called an inverse mask.
Each octet is 0 to 255. A 0 octet must match the address exactly. A 255 octet can be anything. So:
- 172.16.30.5 0.0.0.0 matches that one host only.
- 172.16.30.0 0.0.0.255 matches the whole 172.16.30.0/24 subnet (the last octet can be anything).
Ranges that are not a whole octet

The book uses block sizes for this: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on. Pick the block size that covers the range. The wildcard value in that octet is always one less than the block size. The block must start at 0 or a multiple of its size.
The quick formula that always works: wildcard = 255 minus the subnet mask octet. For subnet mask 255.255.240.0, the wildcard is 0.0.15.255.
| Prefix | Subnet mask | Wildcard |
The book's examples, with the range worked out. Every range below was calculated by script and matches the book.
| ACL line (address and wildcard) | Block size | Range matched |
The book says Cisco seems to like 172.16.16.0 0.0.3.255. Remember it.
COMMON MISTAKE

ADDED Do not start a range in the middle of a block. Suppose you write 172.16.12.0 0.0.7.255. A script check shows the router matches the third octet values 8 through 15, not 12 through 19. The wildcard ignores the low three bits, so the match is the aligned block 8-15. Always write the real network address (here 172.16.8.0).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Wildcard masks do not have to be one solid run of 1s. A mask such as 0.0.254.255 is legal: it ignores every bit of the third octet except the last. With base 192.168.1.0 it matches 192.168.1.x, 192.168.3.x, 192.168.5.x and so on (the odd third octets). Script-checked. This is very unlikely on the CCNA exam, but now you know it exists.
MEMORY TIP
Two shortcuts you must know. any = 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255. host 1.2.3.4 = 1.2.3.4 0.0.0.0. Wildcards work the same in standard and extended ACLs.
Quick check 10.3.1
Q1. What is the wildcard mask for a /26?
Answer: B - a /26 mask ends in 192, so 255 - 192 = 63. Script-checked.
Q2. What range does 10.1.64.0 0.0.15.255 match?
Answer: 10.1.64.0 to 10.1.79.255 - the block size in the third octet is 16. Script-checked.
Q3. Write the line that matches the subnet of host 172.16.50.173/20.
Answer: 172.16.48.0 0.0.15.255 - a /20 in the third octet gives block size 16. 50 falls in the block starting at 48. Script-checked.
Q4. In a wildcard mask, what does a 1 bit mean?
Answer: Ignore this bit - 0 means the bit must match. 1 means it does not matter.
10.3.2 Standard Access List Example

BOOK Book pages 298 to 301. Goal (Figure 10.2): a router has three LANs and a WAN link to the Internet. Sales (172.16.40.0/24) must not reach Finance (172.16.50.0/24). Sales must still reach the Internet and Marketing (172.16.60.0/24). Marketing must be able to reach Finance.
Standard ACL for Figure 10.2 BOOK
Lab_A#config t
Lab_A(config)#access-list 10 deny 172.16.40.0 0.0.0.255
Lab_A(config)#access-list 10 permit any
Lab_A(config)#int fa0/1
Lab_A(config-if)#ip access-group 10 out
- Line 1 denies every source in 172.16.40.0 to 172.16.40.255 (the Sales LAN).
- Line 2 permits everything else. Without it, the implicit deny would block all traffic.
- int fa0/1 is the interface that leads to Finance.
- ip access-group 10 out applies ACL 10 to packets leaving that interface.
WHY THIS MATTERS

Why Fa0/1 outbound? The book explains that putting the ACL inbound on Fa0/0 (the Sales interface) would deny Sales access to every network behind the router, including the Internet. Applying it outbound on Fa0/1 only affects packets that are about to leave towards Finance. Sales traffic to Marketing and the Internet leaves by other interfaces, so it is untouched. This is the standard rule: standard ACL near the destination.
Example 2 (Figure 10.3): Accounting and the HR server

BOOK Goal: stop Accounting from reaching the HR server on the Lab_B router, and let everyone else in. The book points out that the best answer is an extended ACL near the source, but the question asks for a standard ACL, so it goes near the destination. The Accounting subnet is 192.168.10.128/27, block size 32, wildcard 0.0.0.31.
Standard ACL for Figure 10.3 BOOK
Lab_B(config)#access-list 10 deny 192.168.10.128 0.0.0.31
Lab_B(config)#access-list 10 permit any
Lab_B(config)#interface Ethernet 0
Lab_B(config-if)#ip access-group 10 out
The subnet and wildcard were checked by script: 192.168.10.128/27 covers 192.168.10.128 to 192.168.10.159, wildcard 0.0.0.31.
Example 3 (Figure 10.4): block four LANs from the Internet
BOOK Each LAN has one host address shown. You work out each subnet and its wildcard. The book's answer is below. The numbers match the script results.
| Host shown | Subnet | Wildcard | ACL line |
Then permit the rest and apply it to the serial link BOOK
Router(config)#access-list 1 permit any
Router(config)#interface serial 0
Router(config-if)#ip access-group 1 out

The book notes you could do this with one line, access-list 1 deny 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255. It also warns that if you really applied this ACL, you would block all four LANs from the Internet, so the exercise is only for practising block sizes.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

BOOK Four-line answers like this are about exam practice. Check the order the book lists them in (E0 to E3). The text does not say which line belongs to which interface, and the mapping is hard to read from the figure. CHECK It does not change the maths.
Quick check 10.3.2
Q1. Where is a standard ACL normally placed, and why?
Answer: Close to the destination - it only sees the source address, so near the source it would block that source from everything.
Q2. In the Sales and Finance example, why does the list need permit any?
Answer: Because of the implicit deny - without it, every other packet would be dropped too.
Q3. What wildcard matches the Accounting subnet 192.168.10.128/27?
Answer: C - a /27 has block size 32, so the wildcard is 31. Script-checked.
10.3.3 Controlling VTY (Telnet/SSH) Access

BOOK Book pages 302 and 303. You want to stop people from logging in to your router remotely, except from certain hosts. The problem is that every active interface is a possible way in. Putting an extended ACL on every interface does not scale, and it adds work for every packet the router forwards.

The better way: use a standard ACL on the VTY lines. VTY access is already Telnet or SSH, so you do not need a protocol. You also do not need a destination, because it does not matter which router address the user connected to. You only care where the user comes from.
- Create a standard ACL that permits only the host(s) allowed to connect.
- Apply it to the VTY lines with access-class ... in.
Allow only 172.16.10.3 to connect BOOK
Lab_A(config)#access-list 50 permit host 172.16.10.3
Lab_A(config)#line vty 0 4
Lab_A(config-line)#access-class 50 in
- access-list 50 permit host 172.16.10.3 permits one source. Everyone else hits the implicit deny.
- line vty 0 4 enters configuration for the five VTY lines (0 to 4).
- access-class 50 in applies the ACL to incoming Telnet or SSH sessions on those lines. It is access-class, not ip access-group.
WHY THIS MATTERS
The book's sidebar makes the same point: an access-class ACL only checks packets that are trying to log in to the router, so it adds no delay for normal traffic on busy interfaces.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says to use SSH instead of Telnet and points you to "Chapter 6, Cisco's Internetworking Operating System (IOS)". In this volume, Chapter 6 is OSPF. The IOS and SSH chapter is in a different book. Cisco itself recommends SSH, and says the VTY ACL is a way to improve security on the administrative lines. Use an admin subnet, not a single host, in real life, as the book suggests.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
ADDED Extra points about access-class:
1. The out form restricts outgoing connections from the router (for example the router telnetting out to a device). Cisco's command reference describes in and out this way.
2. Modern IOS accepts a named ACL: access-class ADMIN-ONLY in. Older course material says only numbered lists work. CHECK
3. To make the lines SSH-only, add transport input ssh under line vty 0 4. This also needs SSH configured (hostname, domain name, RSA keys, local user). CHECK
4. To see the ACL on a line: show line vty 0 or show running-config | section line vty. The hit counters show in show access-lists. CHECK
WARNING

If your own computer is not permitted by the VTY ACL, you lock yourself out of remote access. Configure it from the console cable or keep your existing session open while you test from a second window.
Quick check 10.3.3
Q1. Which command applies an ACL to the VTY lines?
A. ip access-group 50 in
B. access-class 50 in
C. ip access-list 50 in
D. line access 50
Answer: B - access-class goes under the line, ip access-group goes under an interface.
Q2. Why does a standard ACL work for VTY control?
Answer: Only the source address matters - VTY access already means Telnet or SSH, and the target address does not matter.
Q3. After access-list 50 permit host 172.16.10.3, can host 172.16.10.4 connect?
Answer: No - it matches no line, so the implicit deny blocks it.

BOOK Book pages 303 to 313. Suppose you must let Sales reach one server on the Finance LAN but nothing else on it. A standard ACL cannot do this because it only sees the source. An extended ACL can match source address, destination address, protocol and port number, so it can allow one service on one host and block the rest.
EXAM CRITICAL
Extended ACL numbers: 100-199 and 2000-2699.
The extended ACL line, part by part
One extended ACL line BOOK
access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.16.30.2 eq 23 log
| Part | Value here | What it does |
| Command | access-list | Creates one numbered line in global configuration mode. |
| Number | 110 | 100-199 tells the router this is an extended ACL. |
| Action | deny | permit or deny. |
| Protocol | tcp | The IP protocol to match: ip (everything), tcp, udp, icmp, ospf, eigrp, gre and others, or a number 0-255. |
| Source | any | any, host a.b.c.d, or address plus wildcard. A source port could follow here. |
| Destination | host 172.16.30.2 | Same choices as the source. |
| Port test | eq 23 | Compare the destination port. 23 is Telnet. You may type the name telnet instead. |
| Option | log | Writes a log message every time this line is matched. |
EXAM CRITICAL

Protocol matters. To filter by an upper-layer port, you must pick tcp or udp as the protocol. If you pick ip, you cannot add a port. Telnet, FTP and HTTP use TCP. TFTP uses UDP. permit ip any any permits every IP protocol, but permit tcp any any would permit TCP only and leave UDP, ICMP and the rest to the implicit deny.
Port operators
| Operator | Meaning |
| eq | Equal to this port |
| neq | Not equal to this port |
| gt | Greater than this port number |
| lt | Lower than this port number |
| range | A range of ports, for example range 20 21 |

You can type a port number or a name. The book shows the long list of names that the IOS in its examples understood. Here are the ones you must know. Names in the second group are not in the book's list.
| Service | Port | Protocol | Source |
| FTP data / control | 20 / 21 | TCP | BOOK |
| Telnet | 23 | TCP | BOOK |
| SMTP | 25 | TCP | BOOK |
| DNS (domain) | 53 | UDP and TCP | BOOK |
| HTTP (www) | 80 | TCP | BOOK |
| POP3 | 110 | TCP | BOOK |
| SSH | 22 | TCP | ADDED general knowledge |
| TFTP | 69 | UDP | ADDED the book uses it in a show output |
| HTTPS | 443 | TCP | ADDED general knowledge |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book's help output (page 305 to 306) has no entries for SSH or HTTPS. That is from the IOS used in the book. Newer IOS accepts more names, but the safest habit is to type the number when you are not sure. Name support varies by version. CHECK
Useful options
| Option | What it does | Source |
| log | Logs a message each time the line matches. Great for spotting attempts, but in a large network it can flood the console. | BOOK |
| log-input | Like log, but also shows the input interface. | BOOK (listed only) |

| established | TCP only. Matches packets that belong to an existing connection (the ACK or RST bit is set). Often used to allow replies back in without allowing new connections in. | ADDED general knowledge CHECK |
| time-range | Makes the line active only at certain times. | BOOK (listed only) |
| fragments, dscp, precedence, tos, syn, ack, and so on | Other matching options. Not needed for the CCNA at this level. | BOOK (listed only) |

After the deny line, the book adds access-list 110 permit ip any any. The book is clear about why: if you apply a list with only a deny line, the implicit deny drops everything else, so the list would shut the interface down in effect.
You apply it like a standard ACL:
Pick one direction BOOK
Corp(config-if)#ip access-group 110 in
Corp(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED An ACL is stateless. If you block everything inbound except one service, the replies to your own outgoing traffic may be blocked too. Think about both directions of a conversation when you write a list.
Quick check 10.4
Q1. Why does permit ip any any appear at the end of the book's examples?
Answer: To permit everything not matched earlier - otherwise the implicit deny drops all other traffic.
Q2. Which protocol keyword must you use to filter FTP?
A. ip
B. udp
C. tcp
D. icmp
Answer: C - FTP uses TCP. With ip you cannot add a port test.
Q3. What does eq 23 match?
Answer: Packets with TCP port 23 (Telnet) - eq means equal to. You can type telnet instead of 23.
Q4. What does the log keyword do?
Answer: Logs each match - useful for monitoring, but may flood the console on a busy network.
10.4.1 Extended Access List Example 1
BOOK Book pages 307 and 308. Goal (Figure 10.5): deny Telnet and FTP to the host 172.16.50.5 on the Finance LAN. All other services, and all other hosts, stay reachable by Sales and Marketing.
Extended ACL, example 1 BOOK
Lab_A#config t
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.16.50.5 eq 21
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.16.50.5 eq 23
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 permit ip any any
Lab_A(config)#int fa0/1
Lab_A(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out
- 110 is an extended ACL. tcp is needed because FTP and Telnet use TCP ports.
- any is the source: from anywhere.
- host 172.16.50.5 is the destination: one host.
- eq 21 and eq 23 are FTP control and Telnet.
- permit ip any any lets every other packet through.
- Applied outbound on Fa0/1 because Fa0/1 is the interface that leads to the Finance LAN. Both Sales and Marketing traffic must go through it, so one list covers both.
WHY THIS MATTERS

The book says if you only wanted to block Sales, you would place the list closer to the source: inbound on Fa0/0. That is the "extended near the source" rule. This is why you must study each situation before you place an ACL.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED FTP uses two connections: control on port 21 and data on port 20 (in the classic mode). Blocking port 21 stops the control session, so the user cannot log in to the FTP server, and that stops FTP in practice.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
BOOK The book writes that you could use 172.16.50.5 0.0.0.0 instead of host 172.16.50.5. The router would store it as host 172.16.50.5. Same result.
VERIFY

CHECK Inconsistent addresses in the book. This example uses host 172.16.50.5 and a Finance LAN of 172.16.50.0/24. Later outputs in section 10.5 show the same list as deny tcp any host 172.16.30.5 and the interface as 172.16.30.1/24. These come from different labs mixed together. The idea is the same, but do not try to match the addresses between pages.
10.4.2 Extended Access List Example 2
BOOK Book pages 308 and 309. Goal: stop Telnet to the networks on interfaces E1 and E2, using the four-LAN network from Figure 10.4.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
UPDATED The book says "We're going to use Figure 9.4 again". That is a typo: the figure is Figure 10.4 in this chapter. Verified in the book text and the figure numbering.
Extended ACL, example 2 BOOK
Router(config)#access-list 110 deny tcp any 172.16.48.0 0.0.15.255 eq 23
Router(config)#access-list 110 deny tcp any 172.16.192.0 0.0.63.255 eq 23
Router(config)#access-list 110 permit ip any any
Router(config)#interface Ethernet 1
Router(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out
Router(config-if)#interface Ethernet 2
Router(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out

The wildcards come from the Figure 10.4 subnets: 172.16.48.0/20 gives 0.0.15.255, and 172.16.192.0/18 gives 0.0.63.255 (script-checked). The same ACL 110 is applied to two interfaces. That is allowed: the one-list-per-direction rule is per interface.
EXAM CRITICAL
The book's four checks for a question like this:
1. Is the number in the right range for the type? Extended means 100-199.
2. Does the protocol match the upper-layer service? Telnet is TCP. TFTP is UDP.
3. Does the destination port match the service? 23 or telnet.
4. Is there a final permit ip any any, so other packets are not dropped by the implicit deny?
10.4.3 Extended Access List Example 3
BOOK Book pages 309 and 310. Goal (Figure 10.6): allow HTTP to the Finance server (172.22.89.26) only from Host B (192.168.177.2). Everything else is permitted. You must do it in three lines.
Extended ACL, example 3 BOOK
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 permit tcp host 192.168.177.2 host 172.22.89.26 eq 80
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.22.89.26 eq 80
Lab_A(config)#access-list 110 permit ip any any
Lab_A(config)#interface fastethernet 0/1
Lab_A(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out
| Line | Purpose | Who it catches |
| 1 permit | Let Host B use HTTP to the Finance server. | Host B only |
| 2 deny | Block everyone else from HTTP to the Finance server. | Host A, Host C, the branch office, anyone else |
| 3 permit | Let all other traffic through. | All other traffic, including HTTPS and ping to the server |
COMMON MISTAKE

Order matters. A script simulation confirms it. In the right order Host B gets line 1 (permit). If you swap lines 1 and 2, Host B matches the deny line first and is blocked. The more specific permit must come first.
WARNING

ADDED This ACL blocks HTTP on port 80 only. Modern servers also use HTTPS on port 443. Hosts other than Host B can still reach the server on 443 under this list. A real policy must match the real service ports. A script check confirms that Host A's port 22 traffic also matches line 3, so it is permitted.
VERIFY

CHECK Placement explanation. The book says to break the "extended near the source" rule here, and puts the list outbound on Fa0/1 (towards the Finance server). It says an inbound list on Fa0/0 would let the branch office through. Looking at Figure 10.6, the branch office link and the Host A, B and C switch both appear to connect on Fa0/0. If that reading is right, an inbound list on Fa0/0 would also have filtered the branch office, and both placements would work. The book's reason is not clear from the figure. Outbound on Fa0/1 is a valid answer. On the exam, read the question's requirements and the topology carefully.
Quick check 10.4.1 to 10.4.3
Q1. In example 3, what happens to Host B's HTTP request if lines 1 and 2 are swapped?
Answer: It is denied - Host B matches the deny line first, and the router stops. Simulated by script.
Q2. In example 2, why must eq 23 come with tcp?
Answer: Telnet runs over TCP - a port test needs tcp or udp as the protocol.
Q3. A user on Sales tries ping 172.16.50.5 under example 1's ACL. Is it blocked?
Answer: No - the ACL only denies TCP ports 21 and 23. ICMP matches permit ip any any.
10.4.4 Named ACLs

BOOK Book pages 310 to 312. A named ACL is not a new type. It is a standard or extended ACL with a name you choose, such as BlockSales, instead of a number such as 177. Names are far easier to understand than numbers on a big router. Names also let you insert, delete or edit a single line. That is the real advantage.
Named standard ACL: the Figure 10.2 job again BOOK
Lab_A#config t
Lab_A(config)#ip access-list standard BlockSales
Lab_A(config-std-nacl)#deny 172.16.40.0 0.0.0.255
Lab_A(config-std-nacl)#permit any
Lab_A(config-std-nacl)#exit
Lab_A(config)#interface fa0/1
Lab_A(config-if)#ip access-group BlockSales out
- ip access-list standard BlockSales creates (or opens) a named standard ACL. The prompt changes to (config-std-nacl)#.
- Lines inside no longer start with access-list or a number: just deny ... and permit ....
- ip access-group BlockSales out applies the name to the interface, the same command as before with the name in place of the number.
Illustrative output CHECK
Lab_A#show running-config | begin ip access
ip access-list standard BlockSales
permit any
A number used as a name

BOOK The book then rebuilds Example 3 with ip access-list extended 110. The book says it "named" the list with a number. Technically this is a numbered ACL that you edit in named mode. Cisco's documentation says a number is allowed as the name in this mode, and this is how you edit numbered lists in modern IOS.
Extended list 110 in named mode BOOK
Lab_A(config)#ip access-list extended 110
Lab_A(config-ext-nacl)#permit tcp host 192.168.177.2 host 172.22.89.26 eq 80
Lab_A(config-ext-nacl)#deny tcp any host 172.22.89.26 eq 80
Lab_A(config-ext-nacl)#permit ip any any
Lab_A(config-ext-nacl)#int fa0/1
Lab_A(config-if)#ip access-group 110 out
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
ADDED Editing with sequence numbers. Inside a named (or number-named) ACL you can:
1. Insert a line by typing a sequence number first: 25 deny tcp any host 10.1.1.1 eq 443.
2. Delete a line: no 25.
3. Renumber the whole list in steps of 10: ip access-list resequence 110 10 10 (from global config mode).
The router numbers lines 10, 20, 30... automatically. Plan gaps so that you can insert later. A new line typed without a number goes to the bottom. CHECK on your IOS version.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED ACL names are case-sensitive. BlockSales and Blocksales are two different names. If you apply a name that does not exist, the interface has no filter and traffic is permitted. Check show ip interface after applying.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says in the show-command section that only named ACLs allow single-line edits. Cisco's documentation says sequence-number editing works with numbered and named lists. Use ip access-list standard|extended <number-or-name> to enter the edit mode for either. Verification: official Cisco documentation.
Quick check 10.4.4
Q1. What is the main advantage of a named ACL over the old numbered form?
Answer: You can identify it by name and edit single lines - the book's two reasons: readable names, and insert, delete or edit of one line.
Q2. Which command creates a named extended ACL called WEB-ONLY?
A. access-list WEB-ONLY extended
B. ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
C. ip access-group WEB-ONLY extended
D. named-acl extended WEB-ONLY
Answer: B - ip access-list extended <name> opens the named ACL mode.
Q3. Is WEB-ONLY the same name as web-only?
Answer: No - ACL names are case-sensitive. ADDED
10.4.5 Remarks

BOOK Book pages 312 and 313. A remark is a comment you attach to an ACL, for standard or extended lists. It helps you remember what a line is for. Put each remark in a consistent place, before or after the line it describes, so you do not get confused.
Remarks in a numbered and a named ACL BOOK
R2(config)#access-list 110 remark Permit Bob from Sales Only To Finance
R2(config)#access-list 110 permit ip host 172.16.40.1 172.16.50.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config)#ip access-list extended No_Telnet
R2(config-ext-nacl)#remark Deny all of Sales from Telnetting to Marketing
R2(config-ext-nacl)#permit ip any any
- Numbered form: access-list <number> remark <text>.
- Named form: remark <text> inside the ACL.
- In the numbered list, line 2 permits one host (Bob, 172.16.40.1) to the Finance LAN, and line 3 denies the rest of Sales to Finance. The permit must come first, or Bob would match the deny.
- The book notes that remarks do not appear in show access-list; they show in show running-config. CHECK On some newer IOS versions remarks may also show in show access-lists. Test on your platform.
VERIFY

CHECK Small inconsistency in the book: the remark typed in the named ACL is "Deny all of Sales from Telnetting to Marketing" but the show run output shows "Stop all of Sales from Telnetting to Marketing". The router stores exactly what you type, so the output was edited. Also the typed eq 23 is displayed as eq telnet, because IOS shows names for well-known ports.
Quick check 10.4.5
Q1. Write the command to add a remark to numbered ACL 120.
Answer: access-list 120 remark <your text> - numbered form of the remark command.
Q2. Where do remarks reliably show up?
Answer: In show running-config - the book says they do not show in show access-list. CHECK
BOOK Book pages 313 to 316. Table 10.1 lists the verification commands.
| Command | What it shows |
| show access-list | All ACLs on the router and their lines. It does not show which interface they are applied to. |
| show access-list 110 | Only ACL 110. Also does not show the interface. |
| show ip access-list | Only the IP ACLs. |
| show ip interface | Which interfaces have an ACL set, and in which direction. It does not show the ACL lines. |
| show running-config | The ACLs and where they are applied. |
| clear access-list counters | Resets the hit counters. ADDED (a Cisco command; not in the book) |
EXAM CRITICAL
The Exam Essentials stress this pair: show access-list shows the lists but not the interface. show ip interface shows the interface but not the list contents.
Book output, shortened BOOK
Lab_A#show access-list
Standard IP access list 10
10 deny 172.16.40.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255
20 permit any
Extended IP access list 110
10 deny tcp any host 172.16.30.5 eq ftp
20 deny tcp any host 172.16.30.5 eq telnet
30 permit ip any any
40 permit tcp host 192.168.177.2 host 172.22.89.26 eq www
50 deny tcp any host 172.22.89.26 eq www
- The numbers on the left (10, 20, 30...) are sequence numbers. They show the order the router uses and let you edit lines.
- Even though you typed port numbers, the output shows names (ftp, telnet, www).
- Real routers also show a match count after each line, such as (12 matches), that tells you how often the line was used. The book output does not show this. ADDED CHECK
COMMON MISTAKE

BOOK The book's ACL 110 here is broken. The list in the book's output was built from two different jobs (a Finance block and the HTTP rule from Example 3). Line 30 is permit ip any any, and lines 40 and 50 sit below it. Because the first match wins, no packet ever reaches line 40 or 50. A script simulation confirms that Host A's HTTP to the Finance server matches line 30 and is permitted, so the deny on line 50 is never used. This is a perfect example of the "new lines go at the bottom" trap. Use sequence numbers to insert a line above the permit.
Editing with a sequence number (the book's example)
Insert line 21 between lines 20 and 30 BOOK (output shortened)
Lab_A(config)#ip access-list extended 110
Lab_A(config-ext-nacl)#21 deny udp any host 172.16.30.5 eq 69
Lab_A#show access-list
Extended IP access list 110
10 deny tcp any host 172.16.30.5 eq ftp
20 deny tcp any host 172.16.30.5 eq telnet
21 deny udp any host 172.16.30.5 eq tftp
30 permit ip any any
Typing 21 first puts the new line between 20 and 30. You could delete a line with no 21 the same way.
show ip interface
Output shortened BOOK
Lab_A#show ip interface fa0/1
FastEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up
Internet address is 172.16.30.1/24
Outgoing access list is 110
Inbound access list is not set

The book points at the "Outgoing access list is 110" line. The "inbound" line says not set. The book had applied BlockSales outbound on Fa0/1 earlier, then applied 110 outbound on the same interface. The second command replaced the first. You can have only one list per direction.
Quick check 10.5
Q1. Which command tells you which interface an ACL is applied to?
A. show access-list
B. show ip interface
C. show ip route
D. show access-list 110
Answer: B - show ip interface shows the in and out lists. show access-list shows the lines only.
Q2. Which command shows the contents of ACL 110?
Answer: show access-list 110 - it shows the lines, and does not show the interface.
Q3. You apply ACL B outbound on an interface that already has ACL A outbound. What happens to A?
Answer: It is replaced - one list per interface, per protocol, per direction.
Q4. Why do lines 40 and 50 in the book's ACL 110 never match?
Answer: Line 30 permits everything first - first match wins, and the permit ip any any is above them. BOOK
ADDED CHECK This table is from general knowledge and the rules in this chapter. It was not tested on hardware.
| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |

A fast routine: (1) show ip interface <int>: is a list applied, which direction? (2) show access-lists: are the lines in the right order, and are the counters moving? (3) Recalculate the wildcard. (4) Test with a ping or a connection from a host behind the router. (5) On the exam, check the ACL number range first.

labs.title: Build the network and test a standard ACL

content.text: Topology (from the book's Figure 10.2): one router (a 2911 or similar) with three LANs. Each LAN uses a switch and one PC or server.
| LAN | Router interface and IP | Device |
| Finance | Gi0/1 172.16.50.1/24 | Server-Fin 172.16.50.5, gateway 172.16.50.1 (turn on HTTP and FTP services) |
Steps

- Build the network and set the IP addresses on the devices. On the router, for each interface, use interface GigabitEthernet0/0, ip address 172.16.40.1 255.255.255.0, no shutdown. Repeat for Gi0/1 and Gi0/2.
- Baseline test. From PC-Sales ping 172.16.50.5 and 172.16.60.10. From PC-Mkt ping 172.16.50.5. Expected: all succeed. CHECK
- Create the standard ACL: access-list 10 deny 172.16.40.0 0.0.0.255 then access-list 10 permit any.
- Apply it: interface GigabitEthernet0/1 then ip access-group 10 out.

- Test. PC-Sales to 172.16.50.5: expect failure. PC-Mkt to 172.16.50.5: expect success. PC-Sales to PC-Mkt: expect success. Why: the list only checks packets leaving Gi0/1 (towards Finance). Sales to Marketing leaves by Gi0/2. CHECK (A blocked ping may show "destination host unreachable" or time out.)
- Verify. show access-lists (look for sequence numbers 10 and 20 and, if your version shows them, match counts) and show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1 (look for "Outgoing access list is 10"). CHECK

- Now move the list to the wrong place on purpose: remove it from Gi0/1 (no ip access-group 10 out) and apply it inbound on Gi0/0 (ip access-group 10 in). Test PC-Sales to PC-Mkt. Expected: now it fails too. Why: inbound on the Sales interface blocks Sales from everything behind the router. Put it back on Gi0/1 out. CHECK

Every step has a lesson: step 5 shows placement, step 6 shows the two verify commands, step 7 shows why standard ACLs belong near the destination.
1. Remove the standard list from the interface: interface GigabitEthernet0/1, no ip access-group 10 out, then no access-list 10.
2. Create the extended list:
Lab 2 configuration (HTTP and FTP instead of the book's Telnet and FTP, because Packet Tracer servers offer HTTP and FTP)
access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.16.50.5 eq 21
access-list 110 deny tcp any host 172.16.50.5 eq 80
access-list 110 permit ip any any
interface GigabitEthernet0/1

- host 172.16.50.5 is the destination (Server-Fin).

3. Test. From PC-Sales open the web browser to http://172.16.50.5. Expect failure. From PC-Mkt do the same. Expect failure. Ping 172.16.50.5 from both. Expect success because ICMP matches permit ip any any. CHECK
4. Run show access-lists and note which line counts changed. If your version shows match counts, they should show the HTTP line (or the line you tested) increase. CHECK

Notice you could not do this with a standard ACL: it would also have blocked ping. The extended ACL blocks only two services to one host.

Q7 Why can you not permit only web traffic to one server with a standard ACL?
Answer: It cannot see the destination or port - only an extended ACL checks destination, protocol and port.
Q8 Where should you normally place an extended ACL that blocks Telnet from LAN A to LAN B?
Answer: On the interface closest to LAN A, inbound - extended ACLs go near the source so unwanted traffic is dropped early.
Q9 Which command applies ACL 5 to an interface for packets arriving?
A. ip access-group 5 in
B. access-class 5 in
C. ip access-list 5 in
D. access-list 5 in
Answer: A - ip access-group is the interface command. access-class is for VTY lines.
Q10 Which command applies an ACL to the VTY lines?
Answer: A - access-class <acl> in - entered in line configuration mode.
Q11 What is the wildcard mask for a /29?
Answer: B - 255 - 248 = 7. Script-checked.
Q12 What is the wildcard mask for a /20?
Answer: A - 255 - 240 = 15 in the third octet. Script-checked.
Q13 What range does 172.20.64.0 0.0.31.255 match?
Answer: 172.20.64.0 to 172.20.95.255 - block size 32 in the third octet. Script-checked.
Q14 Write the ACL address and wildcard for 192.168.10.96/27.
Answer: 192.168.10.96 0.0.0.31 - a /27 has a wildcard of 31 in the last octet. Script-checked.
Q15 An ACL has line 10 permit ip any any and line 20 deny tcp any any eq 23. Is Telnet blocked?
Answer: No - line 10 matches first and permits everything. Simulated by script.
Q16 What is wrong with access-list 15 permit tcp any any eq 80?
Answer: 15 is a standard number, and standard lines cannot name a protocol or port - use an extended number, 100-199, for this.
Q17 Write one line that permits only host 10.1.1.1 to ping the 10.2.2.0/24 network.
Answer: A - access-list 101 permit icmp host 10.1.1.1 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 - extended ACL with the icmp protocol. 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 covers the /24.
Q18 Does permit tcp any any allow DNS queries over UDP?
Answer: No - only TCP is permitted. UDP goes to the implicit deny unless another line permits it.
Q19 Which command shows which interface has an ACL applied and in which direction?
A. show access-list
B. show ip interface
C. show ip route
D. show running-config | include access
Answer: B - show ip interface has the in and out ACL lines. (The running-config also shows it, but is not the best single answer.)
Q20 Which command shows the lines of an ACL and, on most versions, the hit counts?
Answer: show access-list (or show ip access-lists) - the counts depend on the IOS version. CHECK
Q21 A router's own ping to a host is not stopped by an outbound ACL on the exit interface. Why?
Answer: A - CLs filter traffic through the router, not traffic the router itself starts - that is a rule from the book.
Q22 ip access-group Guest-Block in is typed, but the ACL was created as guest-block. What is the effect?
Answer: No filtering. The names do not match - names are case-sensitive, and a missing ACL does not filter. ADDED CHECK
Q23 In a named ACL, what do you type to insert a new line between lines 10 and 20?
Answer: A - sequence number such as 15 followed by the line - e.g. 15 deny tcp any host 10.1.1.1 eq 443.
Q24 You apply a second ACL outbound on an interface that already has one. What happens to the first?
Answer: It is replaced - one ACL per interface, per protocol, per direction.
Q25 What does access-class 50 out do under a VTY line?
Answer: Restricts outgoing Telnet or SSH connections from the router - per Cisco's access-class command reference, out restricts outbound connections. ADDED
Q26 Which v2.0 exam objective covers configuring IPv4 ACLs?
Answer: 4.6 - listed as standard, extended, numbered and named. Official Cisco v2.0 outline.
